seen.line: Step into a fictional story with me. You’ll make a choice, then we’ll see what it changes.
You and your accomplice Ravi robbed a jewellery store. You’re both caught. Now you’re in separate rooms.
Your goal is the fewest prison years for yourself. Ravi wants the fewest for himself.
You choose your statement: confess and name Ravi, or stay silent and refuse the deal.
You cannot talk to Ravi or make an agreement. Neither of you sees the other’s statement before choosing. Here’s the whole deal.
If you both stay silent, you each get one year.
If you confess and Ravi stays silent, you get zero years. Ravi gets five. Zero means no prison years.
If you stay silent and Ravi confesses, you get five years. Ravi gets zero.
If you both confess, you each get three years. Let’s see what your statement changes.
Imagine Ravi stays silent. Your silence gives you one year; confessing gives you zero. What do you say?
You stayed silent. Ravi stayed silent too: one year each. Now change only your statement.
Only you changed: 1 → 0 years. Confessing saves you a year when Ravi stays silent.
Now imagine you both confess: three years each. Ravi keeps confessing. If only you become silent, do your years fall, stay, or rise?
You expected “Stay”. Only you became silent: your three years become five. Ravi still confesses, so he gets zero.
Imagine starting at three years each again. Only Ravi stays silent: his years rise to five; yours fall to zero.
Imagine starting at three years each again. Both stay silent: now it’s one year each. That better result took two changes.
Look at Ravi’s choice. If you stay silent, he gets zero by confessing, or one by staying silent. Confessing saves him a year.
If you confess, Ravi gets three by confessing, or five by staying silent. Confessing saves him two years. He faces the same pressure.
You do too. If Ravi stays silent, confessing gives you zero instead of one. If he confesses, it gives you three instead of five.
That’s the prisoner’s dilemma: confessing improves each person’s own result, whichever statement the other makes.
Yet both confessing gives you three years each. Both staying silent gives you one each. Your better individual choices can leave both of you worse off.
One year each is better for both than three each. But one isn’t your best possible result—zero is. Choosing your half doesn’t choose Ravi’s.
Now you run a café near another owner’s café. In this made-up example, you want the most profit today—money left after costs.
You each choose a discount or usual prices, without seeing the other’s choice. Only today counts. All costs are included. Here are the four results.
If both cafés keep usual prices, you each make ₹5,000.
If you discount and the other café keeps usual prices, you make ₹6,000. They make ₹2,000.
If you keep usual prices and the other café discounts, you make ₹2,000. They make ₹6,000.
If both cafés discount, you each make ₹3,000.
Imagine you both discount: ₹3,000 each. The other café keeps discounting. Change only your action: usual prices or a discount?
You ran a discount; the other café still discounts. Profit stays ₹3,000 each. Usual prices alone would leave you ₹2,000.
labels: Hold the other at usual prices

seen.line: Hold your discount; change only the other café to usual. Your ₹3,000 becomes ₹6,000. Your discount gains from their usual prices.
When the other café discounts, you earn ₹3,000 by discounting or ₹2,000 at usual prices. Discounting pays you more.
When the other keeps usual prices, you earn ₹6,000 by discounting or ₹5,000 at usual prices. Discounting still pays you more.
The other owner faces the same choices. Yet both discounting earns ₹3,000 each, while both keeping usual prices earns ₹5,000 each.
Now imagine each discount costs an extra ₹2,000 today. Usual prices cost nothing extra. Everything else stays the same.
With the new cost, both keeping usual prices still earns ₹5,000 each.
If you discount and they keep usual prices, your ₹6,000 minus the ₹2,000 cost leaves ₹4,000. They still make ₹2,000.
If you keep usual prices and they discount, you still make ₹2,000. They make ₹4,000 after the cost.
If both discount, each makes ₹3,000 minus ₹2,000: ₹1,000 each. Those are all the new profits.
Imagine you both discount: ₹1,000 each after the new cost. The other café keeps discounting. What do you choose?
You kept usual prices. Your ₹1,000 becomes ₹2,000; the other café still discounts. You avoid the campaign cost.
What shaped your choice this time? You can leave a note or skip it. I won’t judge what you write.
You kept usual prices: ₹2,000. With the other still discounting, a discount earns you ₹1,000. Avoiding that cost pays you ₹1,000 more.
Even if the other keeps usual prices, yours now earns ₹5,000 versus ₹4,000 with a discount. The added cost reverses which action pays you more.
The other owner faces the same choice. Usual prices now pay each of you more, whichever action the other takes. Both usual earns ₹5,000 each.
The conflict is gone. Before saying “everyone should stop,” check what one person gets for stopping alone—and what makes continuing attractive.
